# ggplot2 {#sec-ggplot2} ## Learning objectives By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: - Control aesthetics and grouping behaviour in multilayered plots. - Use and combine a broad range of geoms, including line and label. - Customise and extend colours, palettes, scales, axes, and legends. - Use facets effectively for multi-dimensional comparisons. - Arrange and enhance plots using patchwork and marginal plots. - Export visualisations with `ggsave()` and make them interactive with plotly. :::{.callout-note} Like @sec-ggplot, this appendix uses the `penguins` data from `files/chapter5.RDS`, which keeps the original `culmen_length_mm` and `culmen_depth_mm` column names (called `bill_length_mm` and `bill_depth_mm` in `palmerpenguins::penguins` and on Day 3). ::: ## Colours, palettes and extensions Colour is one of the strongest visual cues in data visualisation. In `ggplot2`, colours can mark categories, highlight relationships and guide the viewer’s attention. It is also one of the most common sources of confusion and inaccessibility. ### How colour works in `ggplot2` `ggplot2` applies colour in two main ways: - Mapped colour: controlled by a variable in `aes()`, such as `colour = species` or `fill = species`. - Fixed colour: set manually outside `aes()`, e.g. `geom_point(colour = "blue")`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour=species))+ geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your turn :::: ::::{.task-container} * [ ] Change the code above so that all the points are coloured blue.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g))+ geom_point(colour = "blue") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: > A fixed colour is a setting, not a mapping, so it goes outside `aes()`, as an argument to the geom (here `geom_point()`).
:::: ::: ## Choosing effective palettes :::{.callout-tip} Choosing palettes and checking them for colour vision deficiency are covered in more depth in Day 3, Block 1 (Colour and Accessibility) and Block 4 (Accessible colour with colorspace and colorBlindness). ::: Good palettes show contrast and group differences, and stay readable for all audiences. In `ggplot2`, colours that are assigned to variables are modified via the `scale_colour_*` and the `scale_fill_*` functions. To use colour with your data, the most important thing to know is whether you are dealing with a categorical or continuous variable. Choose the colour palette according to the type of variable: - sequential or diverging colour palettes for continuous variables - qualitative colour palettes for (unordered) categorical variables ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/palette.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Colour palettes' width=100%} ::: ::: You can pick your own sets of colours and assign them to a categorical variable. The number of specified colours has to match the number of categories. You can use a wide range of preset [colour](https://www.datanovia.com/en/blog/awesome-list-of-657-r-color-names/) names or you can use [hexadecimals](https://www.datanovia.com/en/blog/awesome-list-of-hexadecimal-colors-you-should-have/). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, fill = species)) + geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") + scale_fill_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ### Using predefined palettes from colorspace The `colorspace` @R-colorspace package offers curated, perceptually balanced palettes designed for clarity and accessibility. You can select qualitative, sequential, or diverging palettes using `scale_*_discrete_qualitative(palette = "*")` or similar functions. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(colorspace) ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, fill = species)) + geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") + scale_fill_discrete_qualitative() + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your turn :::: ::::{.task-container} Explore the palettes available in `colorspace`: * [ ] Run the command `hcl_palettes(plot = TRUE)` * [ ] Choose an appropriate palette and try it for our plot
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(colorspace) ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, fill = species)) + geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") + scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: :::
:::: ::: ### Other palettes - [Generate a palette](https://mycolor.space/) - [Wes Anderson palettes](https://github.com/karthik/wesanderson) - [ggokabeito](https://malcolmbarrett.github.io/ggokabeito/) - [scico](https://github.com/thomasp85/scico) ### Accessibility It’s very easy to get carried away with colour palettes, but your figures must always be accessible. One way to check how accessible your figures are is to use a colour blindness checker, `colorBlindness` @R-colorBlindness. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Check accessibility ---- library(colorBlindness) colorBlindness::cvdPlot() # will automatically run on the last plot you made ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ### Guides to visual accessibility Using colours to tell categories apart can be useful, but as we can see in the example above, you should choose carefully. Other aesthetics you can use in your geoms include shape and size, and you can combine these with colour to make your plots more accessible. Here is a hierarchy of “interpretability” for different types of data: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/list.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Hierarchy of how accurately different aesthetics can be interpreted' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ## Shape ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, shape=species))+ geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values = c(21,22,23)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Colour ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour=species))+ geom_point() + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Colour redundancy ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour=species, shape = species))+ geom_point() + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ## Grouping logic When drawing lines with `geom_line()`, ggplot2 needs to know which points belong together. If it cannot infer groups, it will connect every point in order of x, producing meaningless zigzags. Let’s see how grouping works implicitly, explicitly and in summary form. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ### Implicit grouping via colour or fill Discrete aesthetics such as `color`, `fill`, or `linetype` automatically define groups. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ### Explicit grouping Explicit grouping defines the groups by which lines should be drawn (still in order of x) without relying on other aesthetics or implicit grouping. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, group = species)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: Grouping by `individual_id` instead joins up the repeat measurements of the same bird, so each line shows how one penguin's measurements vary between the years it was sampled. Birds that were only measured once have nothing to join to, so they get no line. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species, group = individual_id)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ### Summary trend lines ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species)) + geom_point(alpha =.8)+ geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Scales, axes and ordering ### Axes limits Now, we'll use `scale_x_continuous()` and `scale_y_continuous()` for setting our desired values on the axes. The key parameters in both functions are: - "limits" (defined as `limits = c(value, value)`) - "breaks" (which represent the tick marks, specified as `breaks = value:value`). Note that "limits" are only two values (the minimum and maximum), while "breaks" are a range of values (for instance, from 0 to 100). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Set axis limits ---- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour=species))+ geom_point()+ geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,240), breaks = seq(20,240,by = 20))+ scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,7000), breaks = seq(0,7000,by = 10)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your turn :::: ::::{.task-container} Pick a more appropriate set of axis breaks:
R chooses the limits and breaks for you automatically. But it is useful to know how to override this when needed. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Set axis limits ---- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour=species))+ geom_point()+ geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(160,240), breaks = seq(160,240,by = 20))+ scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2500,6500), breaks = seq(2500,6500,by = 500)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: :::
:::: ::: ### Zooming in and out We have seen how we can set the parameters for the axes for both continuous and discrete scales. It can be useful to zoom in and out of figures, mainly to focus on one section of the plot. One function we can use to do this is `coord_cartesian()` in ggplot2, where you can: - Set the limits on the x-axis `(xlim = c(value, value))` - Set the limits on the y-axis `(ylim = c(value, value))` - Set whether to add a small expansion to those limits or not `(expand = TRUE/FALSE)`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour=species))+ geom_point()+ geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(180,210), ylim = c(3000,4000), expand = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.callout-important collapse="true"} ## Limits vs co-ords This IS different to setting the axis limits. `coord_cartesian` is like a *zoom*, while `scale` sets the plotting range. Below we use a shortcut to scale with `xlim` and `ylim` - the trendline is now calculated only from the visible/plotted points. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour=species))+ geom_point()+ geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "#1b9e77", "Chinstrap" = "#d95f02", "Gentoo" = "#7570b3")) + xlim(180,210) + ylim(3000,4000) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ### Axis ordering Axis ordering affects how quickly and accurately viewers can interpret data. For example, ordering categories by value shows which groups have the highest or lowest measurements, while random or inconsistent ordering makes comparisons confusing. By default R will order categories along the axis in alphabetical order: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = species)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false"} ## Question What makes the default ordering less than suitable for rapid comparisons? ::: #### Reordering manually To switch the order, use the `scale_x_discrete()` function and set the limits within it (limits = c("category","category")): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = species)) + geom_bar()+ scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Adelie", "Gentoo","Chinstrap")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: #### Reordering by values Or by using features in the `forcats` package: - `fct_infreq()`: orders by frequency - `fct_reorder()`: orders by another numeric variable (e.g., mean body mass) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> mutate(species = forcats::fct_infreq(species)) |> ggplot(aes(x = species)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your turn :::: ::::{.task-container} How could we improve the readability of this plot even further?
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> mutate(species = forcats::fct_infreq(species)) |> # Species on the y axis gives horizontal bars, which are easier to read ggplot(aes(y = species)) + geom_bar()+ # Direct annotation geom_label(stat='count', aes(label=after_stat(count)))+ # reverse order so the most common species is at the top scale_y_discrete(limits = rev)+ # Redundant titles removed labs(y = "", x = "Count") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: :::
:::: ::: ## Facets When it becomes difficult to see the trends or differences in your plot, we can break up a single plot into sub-plots; this is called ‘faceting’. Facets are commonly used when there is too much data to display clearly in a single plot. ### Cluttered plots In the example below it is hard to see the exact distribution of each histogram: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_histogram()+ scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: Facetted panels make side-by-side comparisons easier: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_histogram()+ scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+ facet_wrap(~species) # make facets by species ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Highlighting Plot highlighting, for example with the `gghighlight` package in R @R-gghighlight, lets you: - Emphasise values over certain ranges - Emphasise key groups - Make facetted plots easier to read: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(gghighlight) penguins |> ggplot(aes(body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_histogram(position = "identity")+ gghighlight()+ scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+ facet_wrap(~ species) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ### Nested facets The `ggh4x::facet_nested()` function in the `ggh4x` @R-ggh4x package is used for creating nested or hierarchical faceting in `ggplot2` plots. Nested faceting lets you subdivide facet panels into smaller panels, creating a hierarchy of facets. Here we group the species by their broad diet: Adelie and Chinstrap penguins eat mainly krill, while Gentoo penguins eat krill and fish. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggh4x) penguins |> mutate(Nester = ifelse(species == "Gentoo", "Krill and fish", "Mainly krill")) |> ggplot(aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y = culmen_depth_mm, colour = species))+ geom_point()+ facet_nested(~ Nester + species)+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+ theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Patchwork `patchwork` @R-patchwork lets you combine multiple ggplots, side by side or stacked, without exporting to another program. This keeps everything reproducible inside R. - Use `/` to stack plots vertically - Use `+` to align plots horizontally ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(patchwork) p1 <- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = culmen_length_mm))+ geom_point(aes(colour=species))+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan")) p2 <- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=culmen_depth_mm, y = culmen_length_mm))+ geom_point(aes(colour=species))+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan")) p3 <- penguins |> drop_na(sex) |> ggplot(aes(x=species, fill = sex)) + geom_bar(width = .8, position = position_dodge(width = .85))+ scale_fill_discrete_diverging() (p1+p2)/p3+ plot_layout(guides = "collect") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: You can also add overall titles and adjust layouts: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} (p1+p2)/p3+ plot_layout(guides = "collect") + plot_annotation( title = "Penguin Bill and Body Measurements", subtitle = "Comparing relationships across species" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ### Marginal plots A *marginal plot* augments a two-dimensional plot (usually a scatterplot) with one-dimensional summaries along its margins, typically histograms, density curves, or boxplots. They let readers inspect the joint relationship and each variable’s distribution simultaneously. Conceptually: - The main panel shows how x and y relate. - The marginal panels show the univariate spread of each variable. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pal <- c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan") # density plot of flipper length marginal_1 <- penguins |> ggplot()+ geom_density(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, fill = species), alpha = 0.5)+ scale_fill_manual(values = pal)+ theme_void()+ theme(legend.position = "none") # density plot of body mass marginal_2 <- penguins |> ggplot()+ # body mass on y, so the density runs vertically beside the scatterplot geom_density(aes(y = body_mass_g, fill = species), alpha = 0.5)+ scale_fill_manual(values = pal)+ theme_void()+ theme(legend.position = "none") scatterplot <- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour=species))+ ### now colour is set here it will be inherited by ALL layers geom_point()+ geom_smooth(method="lm", #add another layer of data representation. se=FALSE)+ scale_colour_manual(values = pal)+ theme(legend.position = "bottom") # Layout allows us to have total customisation over the position of our plots layout <- " AAA# BBBC BBBC BBBC" marginal_1+scatterplot+marginal_2 +plot_layout(design = layout) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12b-ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Plotly `plotly` @R-plotly turns static ggplots into interactive web graphics built on the JavaScript Plotly.js library. It preserves ggplot2’s grammar (via `ggplotly()`), but turns each layer into a responsive SVG/HTML element with tooltips, zooming, and panning: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(plotly) ggplotly( penguins |> ggplot( aes(x = culmen_length_mm, y= body_mass_g, colour = species)) + geom_point(aes(fill = species), shape = 21, colour = "white") + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,linetype = "dashed", alpha = .4)+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan"))+ scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "purple", "cyan")) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Exporting safely ### `ggsave` :::{.callout-tip} Saving figures is covered in more depth in Day 3, Block 5 (Saving figures correctly). ::: One of the easiest ways to save a figure you have made is with the `ggsave()` function. By default it will save the last plot you made on the screen. You should specify the output path to your figures folder, then provide a file name. Here I want to save it as a .PNG image file. Always set the `width`, `height`, `units` and resolution (`dpi`) explicitly: the defaults depend on the size of your plot window, so the same code can produce a different figure each time. dpi 300 is good enough for most purposes. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # OUTPUT FIGURE TO FILE ggsave("outputs/figures/YYYYMMDD_ggplot_workshop_final_plot.png", width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300) ``` ::: ### `svg` Not exactly programmatic, but occasionally a lifesaver. If you save your ggplot image in .svg format then it becomes vectorised. What does this mean? Open your image in a programme like PowerPoint and each element of the plot can be edited, resized or moved! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggsave("outputs/figures/test-file.svg", width = 7, height = 5, units = "in") ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/svg.gif){fig-align='center' fig-alt='svg format' width=100%} ::: :::
